claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a high-temperature equilibrium BCC state.
Incipient chemical short-range order forms within the high-temperature BCC state of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Cooling and intermediate-temperature exposure stabilize or enhance the SRO clusters.
SRO clusters act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for secondary phases.
SRO clusters lower the nucleation barrier for secondary phases in the BCC matrix.
Pre-annealing above 1200 °C homogenizes the BCC state while retaining local chemical-ordering tendencies.
The pre-annealing treatment maximizes SRO development relative to direct quenching.
The pre-annealing step permits SRO regions to form and freeze in without complete homogenization.
Lower temperatures generally favor more equilibrium SRO than higher annealing temperatures.
Local ordering reduces free energy and thereby drives formation of a diversified phase assemblage.
Pre-annealed samples with confirmed SRO will develop a larger volume fraction of secondary ordered intermetallic phases than directly quenched samples.
Directly quenched samples retain a more metastable BCC structure without pronounced SRO.
Intermediate temperatures around 900–1000 °C permit diffusion that promotes local chemical ordering without complete homogenization.
Pre-annealing conditions that fully eliminate local compositional fluctuations prevent the proposed mechanism.
Cooling sufficiently rapidly bypasses SRO formation.
Diffuse scattering or local compositional measurements can verify the presence of SRO after pre-annealing.
Chemical SRO can affect structural phase fractions in an alloy.

contradictions.description: The treatment above 1200 °C is described simultaneously as homogenizing the alloy, maximizing SRO, and allowing SRO to freeze in without complete homogenization, while direct quenching from the same high-temperature state is expected to yield little SRO. The distinct thermal history that would create this contrast is not coherently specified.

The prediction is conditional on confirmed SRO, but the stated falsification rule requires that no SRO be detected. Failure to create the proposed mediator is an intervention failure, not a decisive falsification of the claim that SRO promotes secondary-phase formation.
